title: Closing Health Service Delivery Access Gaps with Geospatial Insights
gist: Three billion people — about 43% of the world — cannot reach a health facility within one hour on foot, a gap invisible to standard indicators like facility counts and bed ratios; the World Bank's Geospatial Planning and Budgeting public infrastructure access tool maps walking versus driving catchments and ranks where each new clinic adds the most coverage, showing 5 km driving access ranging from 95.7% in Nepal to 63.6% in Malawi.

themes.theme: Distance is the unmeasured determinant of health access

insights.claim: Three billion people, around 43% of the world's population, cannot reach a health facility within one hour on foot, well short of the WHO benchmark that primary health care be accessible within 5 km of where people live.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Quantifies the physical-access gap that drives health spending effectiveness in emerging markets and the case for decentralized care delivery.
insights.quote: Globally, 3 billion people, around 43% of the world’s population, cannot reach a health facility within one hour on foot.
insights.locator: Half the world lacks access to basic health care

insights.claim: In sub-Saharan Africa access falls to 65% or lower in rural and dispersed areas, leaving large populations outside the WHO's recommended reach.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Rural coverage, not national averages, is where incremental health infrastructure capital has the largest marginal effect.
insights.locator: In sub-Saharan Africa, access falls to 65% or lower

insights.claim: Traditional health-system indicators such as facility counts, bed ratios and spending levels miss the spatial reality of whether facilities are actually reachable by the people who need them.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: The metrics most commonly used to assess health systems are systematically blind to the binding constraint, so country comparisons built on them are misleading.
insights.locator: Traditional indicators such as facility counts

insights.claim: A clinic that appears on a registry may be effectively inaccessible if reaching it requires a four-hour walk, making geographic access one of the most decisive and least discussed determinants of whether health systems deliver.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Registry-based facility data overstate coverage, which matters for anyone underwriting health outcomes off official statistics.
insights.quote: A clinic may appear on a registry, but if reaching it requires a four-hour walk, access remains limited in practice.
insights.locator: Half the world lacks access to basic health care

insights.claim: Modeling both driving time and walking time produces two different coverage maps for the same geography, and a system that appears adequate under driving assumptions can reveal major access gaps when measured on foot.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: A single modeling assumption flips coverage conclusions; demand walking-catchment numbers before accepting any access claim.

insights.claim: Applying a 5 km driving threshold, baseline population access to primary health care stands at 95.7% in Nepal, 95.3% in Serbia, 83.6% in Uzbekistan, 71.8% in Zambia and 63.6% in Malawi.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Country-level coverage spread of over 30 percentage points identifies where health infrastructure investment backlogs are largest.
insights.locator: Geocoding for health facility access mapping

insights.claim: Where nearly everyone can already reach a clinic, the planning priority shifts from coverage to quality and resilience, including proximity to more than one facility.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Defines the next phase of health infrastructure demand in higher-coverage countries: redundancy rather than new build-out.
insights.locator: From insight to action at global scale

insights.claim: The tool evaluates thousands of candidate locations to find where a new clinic, health post, health centre or hospital reaches the most underserved people, and quantifies impact incrementally.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Turns facility siting into an explicit optimization, which changes how health capital budgets can be defended and audited.

insights.claim: Marginal returns to new facilities fall sharply: the first facility in an underserved region may serve tens of thousands while later ones reach far fewer people, though smaller-reach facilities can still be justified where geography isolates communities.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: The efficiency-versus-equity trade-off is now quantifiable per facility, which is exactly the calculation ministries of finance need to ration capital.

insights.claim: The tool delivers decision-ready outputs — coverage rates before and after each proposed facility, maps of newly reached populations, and metrics that feed investment cases and sector plans — so planners need no raw geospatial data or models of their own.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Lowers the analytical barrier to evidence-based infrastructure budgeting in low-capacity governments.
insights.locator: Planners don’t need raw geospatial data

themes.theme: Building the tool: compute, data and partners

insights.claim: Scaling geospatial access analysis is constrained by computing power — Zambia is about fifty times the size of Timor-Leste — which the team addressed using MEGA, the World Bank Group's interoperable computational platform, with the Dutch non-profit Analytics for a Better World.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Compute, not methodology, is the bottleneck for national-scale spatial planning — a quiet demand driver for public-sector analytics infrastructure.

insights.claim: Health facility access mapping begins with OpenStreetMap as the open-source foundation, converted into a reproducible planning-grade facility map, because official facility data are frequently fragmented or outdated.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Open crowd-sourced geodata is now good enough to underpin sovereign capital allocation decisions where official registries fail.
insights.locator: Geocoding for health facility access mapping

insights.claim: An initial version of the tool supported a 2021 Public Expenditure Review for Timor-Leste, demonstrating it could not only map and measure access but optimize new facility placement under tight budgets, and it can now be deployed as a web application for any country using existing global data.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Proven-then-productized: the approach is replicable across countries and customizable to other sectors such as road access.

insights.claim: Inadequate health access is framed not as a health problem alone but as a threat to global productivity, job creation and shared prosperity, with access to care treated as essential infrastructure for participating productively in the economy.
insights.speaker: @wbg_gov
insights.so_what: Positions health infrastructure inside the growth and jobs agenda, which is how it competes for scarce public capital.
insights.quote: This isn’t just a health crisis. It’s a threat to global productivity, job creation, and shared prosperity.
insights.locator: Half the world lacks access to basic health care
